Following on the heels of a similar accident three weeks ago, the incident is encouraging calls for improved safety oversight on construction sites.
The collapse of an unfinished eight-storey building in Kenya has killed six people.
The structure fell on Friday morning in Syokimau on the outskirts of Nairobi. Coming on the heels of a similar recent incident in the capital, the accident has revived calls for stronger safety oversight.
Construction workers were reportedly at the site when the building’s uppermost concrete slab gave way, bringing down part of the structure, according to a preliminary report from Nairobi City County’s emergency team. The report did not establish why the slab failed.
The Kenya Red Cross initially reported that three people had been rescued and one person was reported missing. TV reports later said that five people had been pulled alive from the rubble and taken to hospital.
The emergency report said the number of workers present when the building fell had not been confirmed, leaving open the possibility that others were trapped.
Firefighters and specialist rescue teams were continuing to search for survivors.
Patrick Makau, a member of Kenya’s parliament representing Mavoko, the constituency that includes Syokimau, urged rescue agencies in a post on social media to act quickly.
“Every second counts,” he wrote, offering condolences to the victims’ families.
The accident follows a similar deadly building collapse in the city on October 23, which killed eight people. The twin disasters have prompted calls for tougher construction oversight.
The Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis, a state research body, has identified poor workmanship, inadequate supervision, substandard materials and faulty designs as wider causes of building collapses.

Haiti's Prime Minister congratulating El Salvador's President for a gang crackdown in Haiti has shone a light on the relationship between the two countries. What's going on, and where does the US stand?
Haiti has been engulfed in crisis since 2018, with protests, a presidential assassination and widespread gang violence bringing the country to its knees.
But earlier this week, Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime hailed a major win in the battle against the violence, thanks to "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs."
El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele had earlier said a joint task force between the countries had "destroyed" what he called "the house of Lanmo San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters." He also tweeted out an as-yet unverified video of helicopters firing on a sprawling property.
A number of Salvadoran troops have been stationed in Haiti, nearly 2,000 kilometers from their homeland, since the beginning of 2025, mostly in an attempt to curb gang influence.
Last month, Bukele dispatched more than 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti, ostensibly to rescue four Salvadorans who were ambushed on October 18 and have not yet been found.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Writing on social media platform X, Fils-Aime thanked the Salvadorean military for helping "the fight against gangs." The two nations are, he added, working alongside the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), in an attempt to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority."
The GSF has been operating in Haiti since 2016. But there are doubts to the legitimacy of El Salvador's presence.
"Where the lines are and where the coordination begins and ends between a bunch of distinct entities and security forces is a huge concern about how this actually plays out, and El Salvador are trying to frame it as their choice, their action," Jake Johnston, a Haiti expert and director of international research at the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) in Washington, told non-profit news agency The New Humanitarian this week.
A UN report about Haiti released on Thursday described "bloody turf wars, sexual violence and other horrors, noting that serious violations and abuses continue to be committed across the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in the Artibonite and South-East departments."
It further found that between July and September 2026, at least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured, with more than half of that violence stemming from "ground or aerial operations carried out by security forces against gangs , sometimes with the support of a private military company using drones."
For many observers, this chaos is a major part of the appeal for Bukele, who appears to wish to export his mano dura (iron fist) policy on to foreign soil. The policy saw gang members jailed on a huge scale and a significant drop in the murder rate of a country once notorious for homicide. But Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a Haiti expert from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, told DW earlier this month that Haiti's gang problem is more entrenched. He says using the same tactics as in El Salvador may not have the same result.
"Haiti does not currently have the conditions to replicate the Salvadoran model: Its prisons were emptied in 2024, its justice system is largely paralyzed and criminal groups resemble militias more than gangs, with territory, taxes, weapons of war and political networks that protect them," Le Cour Grandmaison said.
Despite El Salvador being on Donald Trump's list of "shithole countries" that the US president disparaged in 2018 in notorious remarks which he later partially denied , relations between the US and El Salvador have improved markedly during Trump's second term.
The number of migrants deported to El Salvador from the US rose by 98% at the start of 2026 and Le Cour Grandmaison said the US plays "a central, albeit very discreet, role in public life" in El Salvador.
Bukele's move to position himself as an ally of Trump has seen the US president offer him a level of endorsement and autonomy to do what Bukele deems necessary to protect El Salvador's security and that of its troops.
"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. I said: 'Look, you're running your country. You have to do what you have to do,'" Trump said in November.

Tehran has told the IAEA that it is not possible to resume inspections in the current security situation.
The United Nations nuclear watchdog has urged Iran to allow it to resume inspections of its nuclear facilities.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called for Tehran to restore access for its inspectors in a report circulated by the watchdog among member states on Friday, insisting the move is essential to carry out its remit to monitor the Iranian nuclear programme.
Iran has allowed only very limited IAEA inspections since the United States and Israel launched attacks on the country’s nuclear facilities in June 2025. The report said Tehran had told the organisation that it was not possible to allow the inspections to continue amid the current security situation.
The IAEA said the lack of information about Iran’s atomic sites and nuclear material is “a matter of proliferation concern” that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency,” The Associated Press news agency reported.
The watchdog noted that it is “fully prepared to resume its safeguards activities in Iran at short notice”.
The report expressed particular concern about an underground uranium-enrichment plant near Isfahan in central Iran, according to the Reuters news agency.
Tehran declared the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant in 2025 but has not permitted the IAEA access to inspect the facility.
Inspectors still do not know the plant’s precise location, whether it holds nuclear material, or its status under international monitoring rules. The report did not establish that uranium enrichment is taking place there.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi urged Iran to consider limited technical measures that could make inspection visits possible and help restore routine monitoring, the AFP news agency said.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday that Iran remained committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which seeks to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.
But he blamed US and Israeli attacks for limiting cooperation with the IAEA. Since the bombing of the nuclear facilities last year, the watchdog has been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium, the report noted.
The IAEA withdrew its inspectors for safety reasons, and Iran later passed a law suspending cooperation with it.
The IAEA’s inspections are intended to verify that nuclear material is not diverted towards weapons. Without direct access to sites such as Isfahan, the agency cannot independently establish what is happening at those facilities.
However, the report notes that Iran told the IAEA this month that discussion on resuming inspections in the country cannot resume amid “persistent, explicit, and public threats by the President of the United States of America … to commit further acts of armed aggression”.
Iran said that the issue would not be resolved “until the root causes of the present situation are addressed and the essential requirements for normal safeguards implementation are restored,” the report added.
texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75:
The nuclear agency has not been able to inspect any sites attacked by the US and Israel last year
The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.
Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.
In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.
Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.
Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.
Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.
The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.
The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.
"The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.
Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.
Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.
The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.
The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security
The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US were held this week in Abu Dhabi.
Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.
European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.
Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.
The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.
Despite more than two years of on-off talks, the EU has not settled on a choice. But there is a growing view that Europe should not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent.
Paris and Berlin support a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: the European Council’s president, António Costa, and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.
Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”
Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing , a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

Meanwhile, German tabloid Bild has reported on what it says are the key Russian demands put forward in negotiations with Europe, Ukraine, the US.
It includes a number of maximalist demands which would dramatically alter the security landscape for Ukraine and Europe.
We already knew about some of them – for example, Russia’s demand to keep the occupied Ukrainian territories and the entire Donbas region, demilitarise Ukrainian ports and keep Ukraine out of Nato – but there are also some new ones, including a reported request that Nato should not have any bases in the Baltics and that Finland, which only joined in 2023, should be made to leave the alliance.
The list also includes new proposals on Moldova, which Moscow reportedly wants to turn into a federal republic and then force referendums on the future of two of its regions, Transnistria and Gaugazia.
If this list is true – which we do not know that and have not been able to independently verify it – it is probably fair to say that it’s just not going to work and will only anger Europeans at the time when the US wants to get them formally involved in the process.
Ukraine has been repeatedly clear that it has no intention of giving away the temporarily occupied territories, and even less of signing off the parts that are actually still controlled by Kyiv.
And Finland’s defence minister Antti Häkkänen also made it clear that the demand on Finland’s Nato membership has no chance of succeeding.
“ These matters are not up for negotiation. Russia knows that and it’s absolutely outrageous to even suggest this,” he said, quoted by Finnish public broadcaster yle. “Finland will not be forced out [of Nato],” he added.
The chairman of the Finnish parliament’s foreign affairs committee, Johannes Koskinen , told reporters that “if such a paper or demand has been submitted, it will go straight into the bin,” IS reported.
Lithuanian foreign minister Kęstutis Budrys also made it clear earlier this week that Lithuania would block any agreement giving Russia the power to stop Nato deployments in the region.

The bright blue map that emerged on election night in the US was unthinkable two years ago. When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, many Democratic voters curled up in bed and doomscrolled, fatigued and fearful about the direction of the country. Any desire to fight back was dampened by the enormity of the loss.
But the mood gradually shifted over the following two years, culminating in a generational shift on election day: Democrats flipped five governors’ seats and took control of the House and Senate by wide margins. Voters were angry about the rising cost of living, the war in Iran, masked immigration agents in their neighborhoods and datacenters rising in their backyards.

Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing the Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to each food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.
Jan von Plato said he started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.
In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel, and other secondary scientific literature.
“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically, a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.
“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.
Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.
The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.
“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”
Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice he would have won the 1940 Fields medal.
“Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”
In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About fifty were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! or schlecht! [bad].”
Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”
Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”
He said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

Police say allegations of sexual misconduct are separate from those made by multiple women in Guardian and ITN investigation
The Metropolitan police have announced a criminal investigation into David Walliams over alleged sexual misconduct.
In reports by the Guardian and ITV News, Walliams, 55, has been accused by multiple women of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex.
Details of the allegations were revealed after a court rejected a legal attempt by Walliams aimed at preventing publication. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Walliams is one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors.
In a statement announcing the criminal investigation, the Met said the serious allegations it was investigating were separate from those reported by news organisations. “In recent days, the Met has received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s.
“Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers.
“The allegations are separate from those reported by ITN and the Guardian. However, as part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences.”
Det Supt Mike Cagney, whose team is leading the investigation, said : “We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.
“We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process.”
In a letter addressed to journalists working on the media investigation, Walliams wrote: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.
“I realise I did not always take people’s feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.”
He added: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”
The Met said people could report information to police by calling 101 and providing the reference 4900/10NOV26, or by contacting the complex sexual offences unit on 0207 175 2738.

What’s more fitting than a spiral-bound map for a bare-bones two-door pickup?
Whether it’s nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. The startup has a simple pitch : an affordable electric truck with just the basics , leaving owners to DIY and BYOD for everything else, all for a sub-$25,000 starting price.
Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it’s called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review.
That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now.
The Rand McNally 2027 Road Atlas isn’t quite as detailed as the maps being made for automotive navigation by companies like HERE. Those are designed to be read by computers, not people, with rich data on not just places of interest but also live traffic, road conditions, and the accuracy required for assisted and autonomous driving systems. Any OTA updates to the atlas must be applied by Post-it note, and its 154 pages cover the United States, Canada, and Mexico, in full color.
The system is entirely portable, and it’s vehicle-agnostic: you can use it as easily in a Ford, Ferrari, or Fisker as in a Slate. Some might find the idea a little contrived, but having spent some time behind the wheel of the refreshingly simple truck, I think it fits the vibe perfectly. The automaker has added its screenless GPS system to its store for a limited time, and the review copy Slate sent Ars, along with the sticker pack, will be up for grabs in our end-of-year charity drive.

Heinz von Foerster thought population would grow exponentially and “squeeze” us all to death.
As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday’s global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It’s not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point.
It’s not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever.
Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn’t starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, “they will be squeezed to death,” he wrote.
Plenty of scholars objected at the time, dismissing von Foerster’s conclusion as “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd.” The global population did not keep accelerating at an exponential rate; the baby boom petered out just a few years after von Foerster published his paper.
“He got the picture right just as that picture ceased to be right,” mathematical biologist Joel Cohen of Rockefeller University and Columbia University recently told Popular Science . “The all-time peak happened in the early 1960s.” Nor did von Foerster foresee the impacts of longer life expectancy and the sharp decline in child mortality rates.
Nevertheless, the paper was highly cited and received a fair amount of media coverage at the time. As Alan MacEachern, a historian at Western University, pointed out at The Conversation:
The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate—at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s .
Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts—because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.
Doomsday predictions are nothing new; they date at least back to the first century CE, when an ascetic sect interpreted the Jewish uprising against the Romans in 66-70 as a harbinger of the coming Messiah. The Christian religion has produced a ton of incorrect predictions of the end times; among those making them was Martin Luther, who believed the world would end no later than 1600.
Puritan minister Cotton Mather kept updating his predictions, first calling for the end in 1697, then 1716, then 1736. (He would probably have kept updating them had he not died in 1728.) My personal favorite is Mary Bateman, an Englishwoman in Leeds who claimed in 1806 that her hen was laying eggs inscribed with the words “Christ is coming.” It was a hoax: Bateman had actually used a corrosive ink to etch the eggs before putting them back inside the hens.
Astrologers have come up with their fair share of doomsday predictions, usually involving rare planetary alignments and comets, but scientists have not been immune. Jacob Bernoulli thought the Earth would be destroyed by a comet on April 5, 1719, for example. And in 1974, astrophysicist John Gribbin co-authored The Jupiter Effect , which predicted several catastrophes arising from the combined gravitational force of aligned planets. (Gribbin has since distanced himself from that hypothesis.)
There hasn’t been a successful doomsday prediction yet. So relax, once Microsoft is up and running again, we’ll probably all be fine—at least until 2060, which none other than Isaac Newton believed could herald the end of the world. Or maybe it won’t happen until 2129 or 2239 (based on interpretations of the Talmud) or 2280 (based on interpretations of the Qur’an). Or we can cling to the prophecy of a mystic named Baba Vanga, who thought the world won’t end until 5078.
DOI: Science, 1960. 10.1126/science.132.3436.1291 ( About DOIs ).
